questions.question: What is useEffect, and when should you use it?
questions.title: useEffect as external synchronization
questions.direct_answer: `useEffect` runs synchronization code after React commits a render. Use it to keep a component connected to a system outside React—such as a browser API, subscription, network connection, or third-party widget—and return cleanup when that connection must stop. If a value can be calculated during render, an Effect is usually unnecessary.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands the purpose of Effects instead of treating them as lifecycle callbacks for arbitrary code.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an Effect to calculate one state value from other state or to handle a specific button click.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame an Effect as one start-and-stop synchronization process.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: An Effect synchronizes React with an external system.
Its setup runs after a committed render.
Reactive values read by setup belong in the dependency list.
Cleanup stops or undoes the previous synchronization.
Derived render data and user-specific actions usually do not need an Effect.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`useEffect` is a React Hook for synchronizing a component with a system outside React after a render has been committed. External systems include browser APIs, timers, subscriptions, network connections, media players, and third-party widgets whose state must follow current props or state.

The setup function describes how to start or update that synchronization. React runs it after commit. If setup returns a cleanup function, React calls cleanup before running setup again for changed dependencies and one final time after the component leaves the screen. This keeps the old external connection from surviving beside the new one.

For example, a `ChatRoom` can create a connection for its current `roomId`. The Effect connects after the room is displayed, returns a function that disconnects, and declares `roomId` as a dependency. When the user selects another room, React first disconnects the old room and then connects the new one.

The dependency list is not a manual schedule. It contains every reactive value—props, state, and values declared in the component—that the Effect reads. React compares each dependency with its previous value using `Object.is`, and re-synchronizes when one changes.

I first ask whether there is an external system. Filtering a list, building a full name, or choosing visible JSX can happen during render. A POST caused by clicking Buy belongs in that event handler because the action was caused by the click, not by the component appearing. So I use an Effect for render-caused external synchronization, keep each Effect focused on one process, declare its real dependencies, and make cleanup mirror setup. That model is more reliable than translating every class lifecycle method into an Effect.

sections.title: Step outside React for one reason
sections.content: Render code calculates UI and event handlers respond to known interactions. An Effect fills the remaining gap: an external system must be brought into line because a particular committed UI is now present.

sections.title: Think in synchronization cycles
sections.content:
A component may mount, update, and unmount, but an individual Effect has a simpler lifecycle: start synchronization and later stop it. That cycle can repeat many times while the component remains mounted whenever its reactive inputs change.

Each independent external process deserves an independent Effect. Combining a chat connection and an analytics event merely because both happen after render ties their dependency rules together and can cause one process to repeat for the other's changes.

sections.title: Changing from one chat room to another
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as React commit
  participant O as Old Effect
  participant N as New Effect
  participant S as Chat server
  R->>O: roomId changed
  O->>S: disconnect general
  R->>N: run setup with travel
  N->>S: connect travel
```

sections.title: Synchronize one connection
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Effects run only on the client; they do not run during server rendering. Framework data-loading APIs can often fetch sooner and avoid client waterfalls. An Effect is still valid for client-only synchronization, but it should not be presented as the only React data-fetching strategy.

questions.question: How does the useEffect dependency array work?
questions.title: useEffect dependencies and re-synchronization
questions.direct_answer: The dependency array lists every reactive value read by an Effect. After a commit, React compares each dependency with its value from the previous render using `Object.is`. No array means the Effect runs after every commit; `[]` means it does not depend on reactive component values; `[roomId]` re-synchronizes when `roomId` changes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner sees dependencies as a description of code rather than knobs for choosing timing.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Leaving a value out to stop reruns, which gives the Effect an old closure.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain object/function identity and how to remove a dependency by changing the code.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Include every reactive value that setup and cleanup read.
React compares dependencies with `Object.is`.
No dependency array runs after every committed render.
An empty array is valid only when no reactive value is read.
Fix unstable dependencies instead of disabling the Hooks linter.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The dependency array describes which reactive values an Effect uses. Reactive values include props, state, and variables or functions declared inside the component. If setup or cleanup reads one, it belongs in the array. A correctly configured Hooks linter checks that relationship.

After a commit, React compares every dependency with the corresponding value from the previous render using `Object.is`. If one differs, React runs the previous cleanup and then the new setup. The list must have a constant number of inline entries so React can compare the same positions.

The three common forms have different meanings. Omitting the array runs the Effect after every commit. Passing `[]` says the Effect reads no reactive component values, so it does not need to re-synchronize for changing props or state. Passing `[roomId]` links the external process to the current room.

For example, a document title Effect that reads `unreadCount` must declare `[unreadCount]`. With an empty array it captures the initial count and never synchronizes later changes, even though the code appears to work on the first render.

Objects and functions created during render have a new identity each time, so depending on them can cause unnecessary reruns. The first fix is usually to move object creation inside the Effect, move a constant outside the component, or depend on the primitive values actually needed. Memoization is an option when stable identity itself has a wider purpose. I do not suppress the dependency warning to force a schedule. To remove a dependency, I change the Effect so it no longer reads that reactive value. The dependency list then becomes an honest description of when the external synchronization needs fresh inputs.

sections.title: Dependencies follow reads
sections.content: The Effect body determines its dependency list. The list does not decide which captured values are fresh; it tells React when setup must be rebuilt so its captured values match the committed render.

sections.title: Every render creates a closure
sections.content:
An Effect setup function belongs to the render that created it. It closes over that render's props and state. React cannot patch individual variables inside the closure, so a relevant change requires cleanup of the old process and setup of the new closure.

Reference identity explains repeated object dependencies. `{ serverUrl, roomId }` created during render is a different object even if its fields match. Creating that options object inside setup lets the Effect depend on stable primitive inputs instead.

sections.title: Dependency forms
sections.content:
| Form | Setup runs | Typical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| No array | After every commit | Synchronization depends on every render |
| `[]` | After initial commit | Reads no reactive component values |
| `[roomId]` | Initially and when roomId differs | Tracks one reactive input |
| `[a, b]` | Initially and when either differs | Tracks both inputs |

sections.title: Depend on the value the Effect reads
Boundary to remember
sections.content: An empty array means no reactive dependencies, not ‘run exactly once under every condition.’ In development Strict Mode, React performs an extra setup and cleanup cycle to verify symmetry. A remount also starts a new component instance and a new Effect lifecycle.

questions.question: When does a useEffect cleanup function run, and what should it do?
questions.title: Effect cleanup and Strict Mode
questions.direct_answer: An Effect's cleanup runs before that Effect sets up again with changed dependencies and after the component is removed. In development Strict Mode, React also performs an extra setup-cleanup-setup cycle. Cleanup should undo the matching setup: unsubscribe, disconnect, clear a timer, release a widget, or make an outdated request unable to affect the UI.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands cleanup beyond component unmounting.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding subscriptions repeatedly or treating Strict Mode's development check as the bug.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace cleanup before a dependency change and distinguish cancellation from ignoring a stale result.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Cleanup runs before re-synchronization and on unmount.
It must mirror what setup started or registered.
Clear timers and remove the exact listener that was added.
Abort or ignore work whose result has become stale.
Strict Mode's extra development cycle exposes missing cleanup.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A `useEffect` cleanup function stops or undoes the synchronization created by that Effect's setup. React calls cleanup before running the setup again after dependencies change, and it calls cleanup once more when the component is removed. It is therefore not only an unmount callback.

The strongest rule is symmetry. If setup subscribes, cleanup unsubscribes with the same callback. If setup connects a chat client, cleanup disconnects that client. If setup starts a timer, cleanup clears that timer. Cleanup without matching setup is also a warning sign because the two functions should describe one process.

For example, a window resize Effect can add one `resize` listener and return a function that removes that same listener. When no dependency changes, React keeps the registration. When the component leaves, cleanup prevents an abandoned handler from continuing to run.

In development Strict Mode, React intentionally performs an extra setup, cleanup, and setup before normal use. This stress test reveals code that connects twice without disconnecting, leaks timers, or assumes setup can happen only once. The production issue is missing or incomplete cleanup; removing Strict Mode only hides it.

Asynchronous work needs a stale-result rule. If a request API supports cancellation, cleanup can abort it. Otherwise cleanup can mark that Effect instance as ignored so an older response cannot overwrite newer data. Ignoring a result does not stop network traffic, but it protects UI state from an outdated completion. Cleanup should be focused and idempotent enough for repeated cycles. I design each Effect so the user cannot tell whether setup ran once or a setup-cleanup-setup sequence occurred, except for the intended external synchronization.

sections.title: Setup and cleanup form one reversible process
sections.content: Read the two functions as a pair. Setup moves an external system into the state required by this committed render. Cleanup removes that exact relationship before another render establishes a different one.

sections.title: Dependency changes are handovers
sections.content:
Suppose a component subscribes to topic A and then renders with topic B. Starting B before stopping A would briefly leave both sources active. React calls A's cleanup first, using A's captured values, and only then calls B's setup with B's values.

A fetch response cannot always be recalled after it is sent. An `AbortController` can signal cancellation to compatible APIs; an `ignore` flag covers APIs that still complete. Either way, only the currently relevant Effect should be allowed to commit its result to state.

sections.title: One Effect across a dependency change
sections.content: Commit room A → setup A → commit room B → cleanup A → setup B → unmount → cleanup B

sections.title: Remove a listener with the same function
Boundary to remember
sections.content: `window` is unavailable during server rendering. A production component may initialize with a server-safe fallback and read the browser size after mount, or avoid tracking viewport width in JavaScript when a CSS media query can express the layout.

questions.question: When do you not need a useEffect?
questions.title: Render calculations and events without Effects
questions.direct_answer: You usually do not need an Effect to derive data for rendering, respond to a specific user event, reset a subtree, or notify a parent during the same event. Calculate derived values during render, put user-caused work in event handlers, lift shared state, and use a key for intentional subtree reset. Effects are for external synchronization caused by rendering.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can remove common Effect-driven state loops and duplicate sources of truth.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an Effect plus another state variable for a value available during render.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Classify the cause of work as render, event, identity reset, or external synchronization.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Calculate display data from current props and state during render.
Put work caused by a click or submit in that event handler.
Lift state instead of synchronizing duplicate child copies.
Use a key when a different entity needs fresh component state.
Reserve Effects for external systems that follow committed UI.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I do not use `useEffect` merely because code should run after something changes. I first classify the work. If the value is needed for rendering and can be calculated from current props or state, I calculate it during render. If the work is caused by a specific user action, I perform it in that event handler.

For example, a form with `firstName` and `lastName` does not need `fullName` state plus an Effect that updates it. `const fullName = firstName + ' ' + lastName` always matches the current render and avoids an extra render with a stale full name.

Likewise, a purchase POST belongs in the Buy button handler. An Effect that watches an `isBuying` flag loses the information that a particular click caused the purchase and may run again after remounting. The event handler already knows exactly what happened.

When two children need synchronized values, I lift one state value to their nearest common parent instead of giving both local state and Effects that copy changes back and forth. When switching from editing one user to another should clear an entire form, a key on the form can give the new user a fresh component identity instead of an Effect that resets every field.

An Effect is appropriate when committed UI must remain synchronized with something React does not control, such as a connection, DOM API, media player, timer, or external widget. Client fetching can also use Effects, although frameworks often provide data-loading systems with caching and server support. The result is simpler: render calculations have no synchronization delay, events remain tied to their causes, state has one owner, and Effects are reserved for real external processes with dependencies and cleanup.

sections.title: Classify the cause before choosing the Hook
sections.content: Most unnecessary Effects come from mixing four different jobs. Render calculates view data, an event handles one interaction, component identity controls state preservation, and an Effect synchronizes an external system after commit.

sections.title: Why an Effect-derived value shows stale UI
sections.content:
React first renders with the old derived state, commits it, and only then runs the Effect. The Effect sets the corrected value and causes another render. The user may briefly receive inconsistent output, and the application performs two render passes for information it already had.

Calculating during render removes that intermediate state. A pure calculation may run more often, but it cannot drift. If it becomes a measured bottleneck, `useMemo` can cache the calculation without turning its result into separately synchronized state.

sections.title: Place work by its cause
sections.content:
| Work | Correct place |
|---|---|
| Filter products for current query | Render calculation |
| Submit an order after a click | Event handler |
| Coordinate two sibling inputs | State in common parent |
| Reset form for a new user | Different `key` when identity changes |
| Connect to room shown on screen | Effect with cleanup |

sections.title: Remove a derived-state Effect
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A calculation may still depend on an external store or browser API that can change outside React. That is not ordinary derived data; it needs an appropriate subscription mechanism, often a purpose-built Hook such as `useSyncExternalStore` or an Effect inside a custom integration Hook.
